BrandCoverageOut.description:
What became of one brand spelling in the file.

`noProgram` and `unknownBrand` are separate because they need separate actions: the first is a
commercial gap, the second is almost always a mapping fault.
BrandCoverageOut.title: BrandCoverageOut

CanonicalLineOut.description:
One canonical row, on the wire.

Every money, quantity and price field is a **string**, as §3 requires: a JSON number
would be parsed back into a float by every client, which is the precise error the whole
pipeline exists to avoid. The frontend formats these strings without ever calling
`Number` on them.
CanonicalLineOut.title: CanonicalLineOut

CheckRunOut.description:
One check's outcome, whether or not it found anything.

Present for every check on every run: that is what makes the checklist demonstrably
generated from this file. `notApplicableReason` is the difference between "we checked and
it was fine" and "there was nothing to check", which a template cannot express.
CheckRunOut.title: CheckRunOut

DecisionIn.description:
A note is required by the schema, not only by the service: a decision that changes how every
later file is read, with no explanation, is one nobody can review.
DecisionIn.title: DecisionIn

HealthEnvelope.description:
`{"data": {"status": "ok"}}` - BACKEND.md §3's one-item shape.

Declared as a model rather than returned as a bare dict so the OpenAPI document
describes the response properly. A `dict[str, Any]` return annotation produces an
empty-object schema, which generates a `{}` TypeScript type - the frontend then
cannot read `data.status` and the generated types stop being worth generating. §2
calls schemas "one source for validation, docs and frontend types"; this is what
that costs in practice.
HealthEnvelope.title: HealthEnvelope

HealthStatus.description: The payload inside the §3 single-item envelope.
HealthStatus.title: HealthStatus

LayoutFieldIn.description:
One proposed field. Bounds are 1-based and inclusive.

Pydantic enforces types and the cheap bounds so a malformed body is a 400 before any
layout rule runs; `features/layouts/validate.py` owns the rules that need to see the
whole field list at once (overlap, duplicate names, the record width).
LayoutFieldIn.title: LayoutFieldIn

LayoutPatchIn.description:
A complete replacement field list, not a diff.

Whole-list rather than per-field edits because the rules that matter - overlap,
coverage, uniqueness - are properties of the set. A diff would let a client remove
one field and leave the server guessing whether the resulting gap was intended.
LayoutPatchIn.title: LayoutPatchIn

LegacyLineOut.description: One row as the import read it, with what it matched.
LegacyLineOut.title: LegacyLineOut

MappingPatchIn.description:
A partial update: the canonical fields named here, and no others.

Partial on purpose (BACKEND.md §3's PATCH semantics). The UI saves one row at a time,
and P6 proposes a whole mapping; both go through the same merge, and neither can
clobber a field it did not mention.
MappingPatchIn.title: MappingPatchIn

MaterializeAcceptedOut.description: What a `202` says: where to watch, not what happened (BACKEND.md §3).
MaterializeAcceptedOut.title: MaterializeAcceptedOut

ProgramOutcomeOut.description: One program's outcome on this run. The row that makes a `0.00` legible.
ProgramOutcomeOut.title: ProgramOutcomeOut

RunDetail.description: A run plus its stage timeline.
RunDetail.title: RunDetail

RunSummary.description: One row in the runs list.
RunSummary.title: RunSummary

SpecApplicationOut.description:
What this run did with its customer's approved spec.

Published so "no LLM call was needed" is a fact a client can read, rather than something a
reader infers from an absence. `skipCode` and `skipDetail` are how a user finds out *why* a
spec they approved did not apply to the file they just uploaded - which is the question they
will have, and the answer P10 turns into a gate.
SpecApplicationOut.title: SpecApplicationOut

SpecApproveIn.description:
`force` is explicit and defaults to false: overriding a failing verdict is a decision
somebody makes, never something a client does by omission.
SpecApproveIn.title: SpecApproveIn

SpecOut.description: One spec with its document. The document is published as-is: it is the contract.
SpecOut.title: SpecOut

StageTimestamps.description: When each stage completed. Null means "not reached yet", not "failed".
StageTimestamps.title: StageTimestamps

UnmatchedLineOut.description: A legacy row naming a program this customer does not have. Reported, never dropped.
UnmatchedLineOut.title: UnmatchedLineOut

UploadAccepted.description: 202: the file is stored and a job is queued. The work has not happened yet.
UploadAccepted.title: UploadAccepted

get.description: Process is alive. Touches no dependency, so it never fails for someone else.
Database reachable. Raises `DependencyUnavailable` -> 503 via the handler.

The canonical invoice-line contract: version and fields, in CSV column order.

Public and unauthenticated on purpose - it is a published contract, the same one in
`canonical/invoice_line.schema.json`, and a customer's IT team needs it before they
have anything else.

The legacy exports this customer has uploaded, newest first.

Every upload is its own file and its own import, so a second upload of the same export does not
replace the first - the user picks which one to compare against, and the list says how many of
each one's rows matched a program.
This customer's specs, newest first. At most one `approved` per format.
The customer's programs and their commercial terms. Seeded data, never request input.

What this instance has done, and how long the machine actually spent on it.

`elapsedMsToFirstVariance` is **wall clock** from the upload, including every human decision in
between; `machineMs` is what this software spent. On the demo run those are 34,766 ms and
3,535 ms. Both are reported, because reporting only the first and calling it a pipeline budget
would be a claim this project cannot support.

post.description:
Clear this demo's data and rebuild it from the committed fixtures.

The only destructive route in the system, so it carries four guards: off by default, rate
limited per IP, single-flight, and scoped to the demo customer by slug.

**No `Idempotency-Key`**, unlike every other side-effecting route here - the whole point is to
do the work again. The lock and the rate limit are what make a double-click safe.

**202 is now truthful.** It reports `status: "queued"` and nothing destructive has happened by
the time the caller reads it - `service.start_reset` checks the guards and defers, and the
clear and rebuild run on the worker. It previously answered 202 while its body said
`"reseeded"`, which asked a caller to believe two contradictory things; the fix was to move the
work, not to restate the claim. `statusUrl` points at `GET /v1/demo/state`, which reports
`seeded: false` for an in-flight or interrupted reset and `true` once it has finished.

get.description: Whether this instance holds the seeded demo, and whether reset is available here.
Newest first, cursor-paginated. `nextCursor` is null on the last page.
One run with its stage timeline. The URL the upload's 202 hands back.

The canonical CSV, streamed from the database.

The run is looked up first so a 404 is a 404, with a JSON envelope: once a
`StreamingResponse` has begun there is no way to change the status code, and a client
would be handed a `200` with an error inside a CSV.

One page of canonical rows, in source order. Money fields are decimal strings.

`rowNumbers=12,48,91` is the readiness drill-down: exactly those rows, which is how a
finding's example rows become the rows themselves. It is **not** combined with `cursor` -
an explicit list has no next page, and silently ignoring one of the two parameters would
leave a caller believing they had paginated a filter.

What changed since the last approved file, and what a human decided about it.

`200` with `comparable: false` for a customer's first file, rather than a `409`: having
nothing to
compare against is a state this screen renders in a sentence, and turning it into an error would
make every client translate it back.

post.description:
Approve this file's mapping as a new spec version and release the run.

`201` for a new version; `200` when the mapping canonicalises to the spec already approved,
which
is P9's rule reached through this door rather than a second opinion about it.
Mark this file unusable. Nothing is deleted - a rejection has to stay reviewable.

get.description: The rows that could not be made to fit, with the field, the value and the reason.

post.description:
202: the mapping is accepted and the rows are being written.

The completeness check has already happened by the time this returns, so a `202` means
"this will produce rows", not "we will find out later".

get.description: Rows written, rows rejected and the schema version the rows were written against.

The attributed variances, in the documented export shape.

Served as an attachment so a browser saves it rather than rendering it. The shape is
**proposed**, not a contract agreed with any downstream tool - `canonical/GLASS_EXPORT.md`
says so, and so does the About page.
Every finding, and every check that ran - including the ones that found nothing.

post.description:
202: the checks are queued.

Rarely needed by hand - readiness is chained automatically after a materialise - but it
exists so a run whose checks were interrupted can be re-checked without re-materialising
48,150 rows.

get.description:
The checklist a customer's IT team receives, as markdown.

Markdown rather than PDF: it prints to PDF from any browser, it diffs between two runs,
and it pastes into a ticket - none of which needs a new dependency. The filename uses the
mandated vocabulary verbatim, because the words have to reach the artefact and not only
the screen.
One row per program per calendar month, with the engine that produced each.

post.description:
Queue a rebate calculation over this run's canonical rows.

`202` because the work happens in a job: 48,150 lines is not a request-path amount of work even
at 0.8 seconds, and the status URL is how a client follows it.

Honours `Idempotency-Key`. The queueing lock alone already makes a double POST harmless, but a
client that sent a key believes it is getting idempotency, and §3 says an action with side
effects honours it.

get.description:
The engine, the outcome per program, and what became of every brand on the file.

A flat list of amounts cannot carry the three things that make a zero legible - which engine
computed it, whether each program actually ran, and whether any lines were claimed by nobody -
so they live here.
The totals, the staleness flag, and the legacy rows nobody could match.

How much of the variance is explained, and by what.

`byCause` is grouped on the **link**, never on `variances.root_cause`: `duplicate_line` is the
dominant cause of zero variances and appears in fourteen, so grouping on the variance would
lose a whole cause from the chart.

One row per program per month: what they said, what we computed, and the difference.

`?presence=legacy_only` finds the months the legacy system paid for and we calculated nothing
against - a different question from `?cause=`, and the one asked when a total looks short.

post.description: Compare this run's calculated rebates against an imported legacy export.
Explain this run's variances, line by line.

Promote a validated draft to this customer's approved spec for its format.

`201` for a new version, `200` when the draft canonicalises to the spec already approved -
approving twice is a no-op rather than an error, and a new version for an unchanged mapping
would make the version history say nothing. The status code is the honest signal, so it is
set on the response rather than being inferred by the client from the version number.

get.description: One spec, with its document.

The bare document, in its canonical form.

No `data` envelope: this file is meant to be diffed against another copy of itself, and an
envelope would put a wrapper line at the top of every diff. The bytes are produced by the
same canonicaliser that hashed the document, so two downloads of one spec are byte-identical
and `diff` reports nothing.

The lines behind one period's amount, filterable by status.

`?status=skipped` exists so the drill-down does not page 2,251 rows to find the 14 that need
fixing.
How this file is cut into fields. Defaults to the current (highest) version.

patch.description:
Replace the field list, as a new version, and queue a re-profile.

202 rather than 200: the version exists when this returns, but the statistics that
describe it do not yet - they are a job. The response says where to read them.

get.description:
Every row this import read out of one legacy export, matched and unmatched alike.

The variance summary carries the unmatched rows, capped, for the file a comparison used. This
answers the different question - what did you actually read out of my file - which is the one
asked when a number looks wrong.

delete.description: Remove canonical fields from the draft - the UI's "ignore this column".

get.description: The current mapping draft and the verdicts last computed for it.

patch.description: Update the canonical fields named in the body, leaving the rest untouched.

post.description:
Ask the model for a mapping, or serve the one we already paid for.

Blocks for up to the configured LLM timeout rather than returning 202 and a job. A
named deviation from BACKEND.md §6's 500 ms write budget: this is a user-initiated
action the user is actively watching behind a spinner, with a hard timeout, and the
alternative is more machinery for something already on screen.
Check the draft against a sample of the real file. Synchronous: it samples.

get.description: Every column's profile for one file, in column order.

post.description:
202, not 201: the file is accepted and queued, and the work has not happened yet.

The response carries a `statusUrl` rather than a result, which is what §3 asks of a
202 - the client polls that instead of holding a connection open for a 15-second
parse.

get.description: The source lines behind one variance, each with its contribution and the evidence.
